**Document type and parties**
Auditor's Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC, signed by Chris Geck, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager), dated October 28, 2024, accompanying the June 30, 2024 audit of Troy School District. The engagement letter is dated June 17, 2024; audit planning matters were communicated at a meeting on August 27, 2024; the management representation letter is dated October 28, 2024. The auditors thank Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the business office.

**Results of the Audit**
The audit was conducted under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States. A separate letter dated October 28, 2024 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance. No new accounting policies were adopted and existing policies were unchanged during 2024. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net pension liability and the OPEB net asset under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated at June 30, 2024 at $288.9 million and $4.9 million respectively, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. There were no disagreements with management, no consultations with other independent accountants, and management corrected all identified misstatements.

**Other Recommendations and Observations**
Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance continues to exceed the USDA maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

**School funding landscape**

| Item | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| 2023/2024 target foundation allowance | $9,608 per pupil (increase of $458, 5 percent) |
| Cyber school foundation allowance | $9,150 (no increase) |
| 2024/2025 target foundation allowance | Stays at $9,608 per pupil |
| MPSERS contribution rate 2024 | 48 percent of payroll, up from 45 percent |
| Net MPSERS cost to District | From 28 percent to approximately 31 percent |
| Retirement-driven resources freed up, 2024/2025 | About $400 per pupil |
| Foundation increases in pre-conference bill versions | $217 to $302 per pupil |
| Statewide historical OPEB UAAL cost | About $669 million |
| Redirected under 2024/2025 School Aid Bill (categorical 147a4) | $598 million, approximately 5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll |
| At-risk funding | Now over $1 billion |

Pupil counts used 90 percent weighting for October 2023 and 10 percent for February 2023, with Section 29 support for declining-enrollment districts. ARP ESSER III sunset September 30, 2024. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million; pre-pandemic decline ran about 10,000 students per year, and the pandemic decrease exceeded 50,000 students. On average about 10 students fully fund a teacher position. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference was set for January 2025.

**Michigan School Meals and Food Service**
For 2023/2024 the District received $3,676,677 in state funding under Section 30d for universal free breakfast and lunch. Participation requires application through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system, adoption of the Community Eligibility Provision, and write-off of outstanding student negative balances funded from outside the Food Service Fund.

**MPSERS plan status at September 30, 2023**
Net pension liability approximately $32.4 billion, a decrease of approximately 15 percent from $37.9 billion at September 30, 2022. Net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million, versus a net OPEB liability of $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022. Annual investment rate of return was 8.3 percent for the year ended September 30, 2023 compared with an investment loss of 4.8 percent for the year ended September 30, 2022.

**District fund balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $4.2 million in 2023/2024, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $36.8 million at June 30, 2024. The statewide average at June 30, 2023 was approximately 21.86 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, roughly 11 weeks of operating costs. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.21 percent, approximately 10 weeks of operation.

**Other informational items**
GASB 101 (Compensated Absences) and GASB 102 (Certain Risk Disclosures) are effective for the year ending June 30, 2025; GASB 103 (Financial Reporting Model Improvements) for June 30, 2026. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 permits transportation-related uses for millages approved after May 7, 2023. Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4. The District determined an arbitrage liability of $3,693,631, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit and Type A thresholds from $750,000 to $1 million and the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Identification and transmittal**
Troy School District, Report to the Board of Education, June 30, 2024, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC and signed by Chris Geck, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The cover letter and each section letter are dated October 28, 2024. The report is organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The auditors extend thanks to Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to normal daily activities.

**Results of the Audit**
Plante & Moran audited the financial statements of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024 and issued its report thereon dated October 28, 2024. As stated in the engagement letter dated June 17, 2024, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with board oversight are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States; a separate letter dated October 28, 2024 addresses the consideration of internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with certain provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit was performed according to the planned scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting on August 27, 2024.

Significant audit findings: the significant accounting policies used are described in Note 2 to the financial statements; no new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2024. The most sensitive estimates affecting the financial statements were the District's share of the MPSERS net liability for the pension plan and net asset for the other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plan recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. The District's estimates as of June 30, 2024 were $288.9 million for the pension plan and $4.9 million for the OPEB plan, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered; no disagreements with management arose; management corrected all accumulated known and likely misstatements other than trivial ones; representations are contained in the management representation letter dated October 28, 2024; there were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

**Other Recommendations and Observations**
Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance of the Food Service Fund continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures. The District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level. The same observation is repeated in the Informational Items section.

**2023/2024 state funding**
The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference identified significant new resources. Key highlights: the target foundation allowance increased by $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving the $458 increase; cyber schools received no increase and continued at $9,150. The traditional blended pupil count continued with 90 percent weighting for the October 2023 count and 10 percent for the February 2023 count, with a two-year blended count provision for declining enrollment districts qualifying where the 2023 final membership count was lower than the 2022 final count, funded through Section 29. Special education funding became fully categorical and was provided from Section 51 rather than partly from Section 20. For MPSERS in 2024, the overall contribution rate increased to 48 percent of payroll from 45 percent, with the net cost to the District increasing from 28 percent to approximately 31 percent, the first increase in the District's net cost in several years. GSRP reimbursement was funded at the level of the target foundation allowance with increased income limits. Section 31a/At-Risk funding increased with an opportunity index. Section 30d provided universal free breakfast and lunch. Additional transportation funding used a formula based on riders per square mile. One-time infusions covered student mental health and school safety and a student loan repayment program for employees working directly with students, the latter arriving late in the school year and creating revenue recognition challenges at June 30, 2024. Retirement contributions and ISD operations (up 5 percent) also increased.

**2024/2025 state funding**
The May 2024 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs but slower School Aid Fund growth, closer to pre-pandemic levels. The School Aid Bill kept the target foundation allowance at $9,608 per pupil, continued declining-enrollment smoothing, continued funding the State's Headlee Amendment obligation from the special education allocation, and revised Section 147 MPSERS categoricals. The retirement changes free up about $400 per pupil for operations, though not every district realizes the full benefit; prior versions of the bill before conference committee provided foundation increases ranging from $217 to $302 per pupil. The OPEB plan is now considered fully funded; state funding covers the historical OPEB UAAL cost of about $669 million statewide, and the 2024/2025 bill redirects $598 million of the savings back to districts through categorical 147a4, representing approximately 5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll. GSRP eligibility extends to families under four times the federal poverty level. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations continue without substantive change; the most significant reduction was for mental health and school safety.

**Looking forward**
ARP ESSER III, funded under the Education Stabilization Fund, sunset September 30, 2024, creating the funding cliff. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students; pre-pandemic decline was about 10,000 students per year, while the pandemic saw a decrease in excess of 50,000 students, a portion of which has returned. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference was scheduled for January 2025. Listed challenges include ESSER III utilization, staff and student retention, pupil count trends, learning loss programs, expanded GSRP facilities, food service operations, inflation, technology costs, and school security and mental health staffing.

**Michigan School Meals**
For 2023/2024 the District received $3,676,677 in state funding under Section 30d. Participation is not automatic; districts apply using the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system. Eligibility requires being a public school, charter school, or ISD; participating in the National School Lunch Program; serving breakfast and lunch; serving all meals at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students; adopting the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) to maximize federal reimbursement; collecting family income information; and writing off all outstanding student negative balances, which the Food Service Fund is not allowed to absorb.

**MPSERS plan status**
The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2023 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $32.4 billion, a decrease of approximately 15 percent from $37.9 billion at September 30, 2022. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million compared with a net OPEB liability of $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022, flipping from a net liability to a net asset. The annual investment rate of return was 8.3 percent for the year ended September 30, 2023, compared with an investment loss of 4.8 percent for the year ended September 30, 2022.

**Fund balance**
During 2023/2024, General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $4.2 million, increasing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $36.8 million at June 30, 2024. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2023 was approximately 21.86 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would approximately equal average operating costs for an 11-week period. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.21 percent and equals approximately 10 weeks of operation.

**Upcoming pronouncements and compliance items**
GASB Statement No. 101 (Compensated Absences) is effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requiring a compensated absence liability in the full accrual statements using each employee's pay rate at the statement date, with cumulative effects on net assets as of July 1, 2024. GASB Statement No. 102 (Certain Risk Disclosures) is effective for the June 30, 2025 year end. GASB Statement No. 103 (Financial Reporting Model Improvements), affecting Statement 34, MD&A, proprietary fund presentation, budgetary comparisons, major component units, and unusual or infrequent items, is effective for the June 30, 2026 year end. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows sinking fund millages approved after May 7, 2023 to fund student transportation vehicles, parts, supplies, and equipment, and trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately with an annual independent audit. Michigan Department of Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4, effective for sinking fund and bond compliance audits reported for the June 30, 2024 period; the completion date is the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent. On arbitrage, the District completed its analysis and determined an arbitrage liability of $3,693,631, reported as a liability in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024. The Inflation Reduction Act, signed August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over 10 years to energy and climate projects aiming to reduce emissions by approximately 40 percent by 2030, with direct-payment options for tax-exempt entities and credits available through 2032. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions increase the single audit threshold and the Type A program threshold from $750,000 to $1 million, effective for fiscal year ends starting on or after October 1, 2024 and therefore applicable to the District's fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, with administrative changes effective for grants received on or after October 1, 2024; the equipment capitalization threshold rises from $5,000 to $10,000. Additional advisory items cover grants management risk assessment, cyber threats and the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed in October 2021, operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, and data analytics.

Under the engagement letter dated June 17, 2024, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with board oversight are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States; a separate letter dated October 28, 2024 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. Scope and timing followed the planning meeting of August 27, 2024. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net pension liability and the OPEB net asset recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated as of June 30, 2024 at $288.9 million and $4.9 million respectively, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education to reduce the balance to an acceptable level. The same item is repeated in the Informational Items section.

SCHOOL AID, 2023/2024. The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference identified significant new resources. The target foundation allowance rose $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase; hold harmless districts also received the $458 increase; cyber schools received no increase and continued at $9,150. The blended pupil count continued at 90 percent weighting for the October 2023 count and 10 percent for the February 2023 count, with a two-year blend for declining enrollment districts whose 2023 final membership count was lower than the 2022 final count, funded through Section 29. Special education funding became fully categorical from Section 51 of the State Aid Act rather than partly from Section 20, and no longer supplements Headlee Amendment payments from the foundation allowance. The MPSERS overall contribution rate increased to 48 percent of payroll from 45 percent, with the District's net cost rising from 28 percent to approximately 31 percent, the first such increase in several years. GSRP reimbursement was funded at the target foundation allowance level with higher income limits; Section 31a/At-Risk funding increased using an opportunity index; Section 30d provided universal free breakfast and lunch, state funded and not replacing the federal Child Nutrition Cluster; transportation funding used a riders-per-square-mile formula; one-time funds supported mental health and school safety and a student loan repayment program, funded late in the year and creating revenue recognition challenges at June 30, 2024; and ISD operations funding rose 5 percent.

SCHOOL AID, 2024/2025. The May 2024 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs but slower growth, closer to pre-pandemic levels. The enacted bill provided no foundation allowance increase, holding the target at $9,608 per pupil; instead modifications, primarily to retirement funding, free up about $400 per pupil for operations, though not every district realizes the full $400. Before the conference report, each version of the bill provided a foundation increase ranging from $217 to $302 per pupil. Declining enrollment smoothing continues; the State's Headlee obligation is funded from the special education allocation; Section 147 MPSERS categoricals were revised to increase retirement funding. OPEB is now considered fully funded; state funding covers the historical OPEB UAAL of about $669 million statewide, and the bill redirects $598 million of the savings back to districts through categorical 147a4, representing approximately 5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll. GSRP eligibility extends to families below four times the federal poverty level. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion with new flexibility provisions. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations support continue without substantive change; many smaller categoricals were eliminated or reduced, the most significant reduction being mental health and school safety.

LOOKING FORWARD. The May 2024 conference looked into 2025, 2026, and 2027 and indicated funding levels are leveling off. ARP ESSER III, funded under the Education Stabilization Fund, sunset September 30, 2024, creating a funding cliff. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students; pre-pandemic annual declines ran about 10,000 students per year, while pandemic-era statewide enrollment decreased in excess of 50,000 students, with only partial recovery expected. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. Listed challenges include recession impact, ESSER III utilization, staff and student retention, learning loss programs, expanded GSRP facilities, inflation and technology costs, and security and mental health staffing. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference occurs in January 2025.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL MEALS. For 2023/2024 the District received $3,676,677 in state funding under Section 30d, supporting the Food Service Fund and replacing revenue previously received from student-paid meals. Districts apply through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system and must participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), collect family income information, and write off outstanding student negative balances, funded from sources outside the Food Service Fund under MDE guidance.

GRANTS MANAGEMENT AND MPSERS. Title I, Special Education, and Child Nutrition, plus pandemic programs ESSER, GEER, and CRF, have increased workload and grants management risk; the auditor suggests a risk assessment of key processes and controls in fiscal year 2025. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2023 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $32.4 billion, a decrease of approximately 15 percent from $37.9 billion at September 30, 2022, driven by net investment returns; the annual investment rate of return was 8.3 percent for the year ended September 30, 2023 compared with an investment loss of 4.8 percent for the year ended September 30, 2022. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million at September 30, 2023 compared with a net OPEB liability of $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022.

FUND BALANCE. During 2023/2024 the District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $4.2 million, increasing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $36.8 million at June 30, 2024. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2023 was approximately 21.86 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, equal to about an 11-week period of operating costs. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.21 percent and equals approximately 10 weeks of operation.

UPCOMING PRONOUNCEMENTS. GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, requires a full accrual liability for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the statement date, replacing gross additions and reductions disclosure with net change and removing the disclosure of which funds liquidate the liability; effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, including cumulative effects on net assets as of July 1, 2024. GASB Statement No. 102, Certain Risk Disclosures, effective June 30, 2025, requires disclosure of concentrations or constraints, related events, and mitigating actions. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, effective June 30, 2026, revises Statement 34 reporting: MD&A limited to five topics, proprietary fund operating/nonoperating definitions with a new subtotal for operating income (loss) and noncapital subsidies, budgetary comparisons reported only in required supplementary information, separate major component unit presentation, and separate presentation of unusual or infrequent items.

SINKING FUNDS AND TREASURY GUIDANCE. Legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows a sinking fund millage approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to fund acquisition of student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and equipment, and trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923, used for building maintenance. Sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately, each with its own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balance, and an annual independent sinking fund audit is required. Michigan Department of Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 effective for compliance audits reported for the June 30, 2024 reporting period; Plante & Moran participated in reviewing the guidance. Districts no longer submit financial information at bond closeout but must submit an annual transmittal letter on the bond-funded Capital Projects Fund; the completion date is the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent; multiple series approved by electors at the same time may be accounted for in one fund; and levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be in a capital projects fund separate from balances from levies authorized before that date.

ARBITRAGE AND OTHER ITEMS. Arbitrage is the difference between interest expense paid by the bond issuer and earnings on invested bond proceeds, with a computation generally completed at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale for reporting excess earnings to the Internal Revenue Service. The District has unspent bond proceeds accruing investment earnings at June 30; its analysis determined an arbitrage liability of $3,693,631, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024. The Inflation Reduction Act, signed August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over 10 years for energy and climate projects targeting roughly 40 percent emissions reduction by 2030, and offers tax-exempt entities a direct-payment option for qualifying capital improvements such as certain electric vehicles and solar panels, with many credits available through 2032. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit threshold and the Type A program threshold from $750,000 to $1 million, effective for fiscal year ends starting on or after October 1, 2024 and therefore applicable to the District's fiscal year ending June 30, 2026; the equipment capitalization threshold rises from $5,000 to $10,000, with tracking still required below that if District policy is set lower. Closing advisory items address cyber threats (citing the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed in October 2021 and PII, FERPA, HIPAA, and PCI data), operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, and data analytics.

**Resolution text**
The resolution enrolls the named schools as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc. and further enrolls them to participate in approved interschool athletic activities. The Board delegates to the Superintendent or designee the responsibility for supervision and control of those activities, accepts the association's Constitution and By-Laws, and adopts its rules, regulations and interpretations as published in the current Handbook as minimum standards and the governing code, agreeing to primary enforcement. The authorization runs from August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025 and may not be revoked during that period. A Record of Adoption block provides for the school name, the day and month in 2024, the governing body name, address, city and zip, contact e-mail, and the Board Secretary or designee signature.

**Membership eligibility rules**
Membership requires a school building with enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students, for grades 6 through 8 or 9, 7 through 8 or 9, or 9 or 10 through 12; nonpublic schools must qualify for federal income tax exemption as a not-for-profit organization. Schools may join at the sixth-grade level to reach the 15-student minimum whether or not sixth graders participate in athletics. Section A states the rules do not require districts to become members at the junior high or middle school level, nor to sponsor interscholastic athletics for sixth graders. Section B states that if a listed junior high or middle school sponsors a sixth-grade team in any sport or permits a sixth grader to participate with seventh and eighth graders, all of Regulations III and IV apply to all sixth graders in all sports involving sixth graders on that school's teams; if no sixth graders participate in a sport, MHSAA rules do not apply in that sport.

ORGANIZATIONAL DESCRIPTION. The form describes the Michigan High School Athletic Association as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation comprised of public, private and parochial junior high, middle and senior high schools whose Boards of Education or Governing Bodies have voluntarily applied for and received membership for and on behalf of their secondary schools. The association sponsors statewide tournaments and makes eligibility rules with respect to participation in MHSAA-sponsored tournaments in the various sports. Each Board of Education or Governing Body that wishes to host or participate in such meets and tournaments must join the MHSAA and agree to abide by and enforce the MHSAA rules, regulations and qualifications concerning eligibility, game rules and tournament policies, procedures and schedules. It is a condition of participation in any MHSAA postseason tournament that high schools adhere to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports.

PROPRIETARY RIGHTS. The form states that MHSAA tournaments are the collective property of the MHSAA and not of any individual member school, and that the MHSAA reserves the right to promote and advance the membership's interests with publication information; exclusive arrangements to create recognition and exposure for school-sponsored activities; restrictive policies prohibiting exploitation and commercialization of MHSAA-sponsored tournaments; appropriate proprietary interests; and the use of images or transmissions identifying contest officials, spectators and member schools' students, personnel and marks.

ADOPTION MECHANICS. To obtain membership, the Board of Education or Governing Body must adopt the resolution for its junior high, middle and senior high schools. The resolution must be formally ratified by the Board and properly signed, with one signed copy returned to the MHSAA for its files and one retained by the district. Resolutions that are modified in any way or supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on MHSAA membership or tournament participation shall be rejected.

MEMBERSHIP RESOLUTION. The resolution is stated to be for the year August 1, 2024 through July 31, 2025. It provides blanks for the school or schools under the direction of the Board, the city or township, and the county in the State of Michigan, and declares those schools (A) enrolled as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc., a nonprofit association, and (B) further enrolled to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities sponsored by the association. The Board of Education or Governing Body delegates to the Superintendent or designee the responsibility for the supervision and control of those activities, accepts the Constitution and By-Laws of the association, and adopts as its own the rules, regulations and interpretations as minimum standards, as published in the current Handbook, as the governing code under which the schools shall conduct their program of interscholastic athletics, agreeing to primary enforcement of those rules, regulations, interpretations and qualifications. Schools that host or participate in the association's meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures and schedules. The authorization is effective from August 1, 2024 and remains effective until July 31, 2025, during which the authorization may not be revoked.

MEMBERSHIP ELIGIBILITY NOTE. Pursuant to the MHSAA Constitution, all high schools, junior high or middle schools, or other schools of Michigan doing a corresponding grade of work may become members provided (a) the school building has enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students, whether for grades 6 through 8 or 9, grades 7 through 8 or 9, or grades 9 or 10 through 12; and (b) if a nonpublic school, the school qualifies for federal income tax exemption as a not-for-profit organization. To reach the 15-student minimum for middle school membership, schools may join the MHSAA at the sixth-grade level whether or not sixth-grade students participate in athletics. Paragraph A states that the section does not require school districts to become member schools at the junior high or middle school level and does not require them to sponsor any interscholastic athletics for sixth-grade students. Paragraph B states that if a school district's MHSAA Membership Resolution lists a junior high or middle school as an MHSAA member school, and if the school sponsors a sixth-grade team in any sport or permits a sixth-grade student to participate with seventh- and eighth-grade students in any sport, then all of Regulations III and IV apply to all sixth-graders in all sports involving sixth-graders on teams sponsored by that school; if the school does not allow any sixth-graders to participate in a sport, MHSAA rules do not apply in that sport.
